method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: QUOTED from Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand (TSANZ), Respirology 2024 'Treatment of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and progressive pulmonary fibrosis: A position statement from the Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand 2023 revision' (published online 11 January 2024), 26 claims; LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC10952210). S2: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from Raghu G, Remy-Jardin M, Richeldi L, et al., American Thoracic Society, European Respiratory Society, Japanese Respiratory Society and Asociación Latinoamericana de Tórax, American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine 205(9):e18-e47 (doi 10.1164/rccm.202202-0399ST) 'Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (an Update) and Progressive Pulmonary Fibrosis in Adults: An Official ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT Clinical Practice Guideline' (published 1 May 2022), 10 claims; LICENCE: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; Copyright © 2022 by the American Thoracic Society ('You may print one copy of this document at no charge. However, if you require more than one copy, you must place a reprint order.') (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> and <copyright-statement> elements for PMC9851481). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Edition 2.0 adds S2, the ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT 2022 guideline, paraphrased because it is CC BY-NC-ND, mainly for diagnosis (outside S1's scope) and the international management pathway. It is the most recent open international IPF/PPF guideline found (the German S2k 2024 and Korean 2026 guidelines are paywalled); it predates nerandomilast, as does S1. The S1 claims and fragments are unchanged. Table rows appended with pmc_text.py --append-tables (2026-09-24); claims from S1 Tables 4–6 (acute-exacerbation criteria, vasodilator trials, short-telomere features; quoted) and S2 Table 5 (fibrotic ILDs that can manifest PPF; paraphrased) are anchored to their row lines. S1 Tables 1–2 (doses, PBS criteria; ragged rows) and S2 Tables 2–4 (merged cells) were not extracted.

claims.claim: **Suspect IPF** when there is unexplained bilateral fibrosis on chest X-ray or CT with bibasilar inspiratory crackles in someone over 60 years; people aged 40 to 60 occasionally present the same way, especially with features of familial pulmonary fibrosis.
claims.locator: Raghu G, Remy-Jardin M, Richeldi L, et al., American Thoracic Society, European Respiratory Society, Japanese Respiratory Society and Asociación Latinoamericana de Tórax, American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine 205(9):e18-e47 (doi 10.1164/rccm.202202-0399ST), 'Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (an Update) and Progressive Pulmonary Fibrosis in Adults: An Official ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT Clinical Practice Guideline', published 1 May 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9851481/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **A probable UIP pattern on HRCT is now handled like a definite UIP pattern:** in the right clinical setting (for example a 60-year-old male smoker), multidisciplinary discussion can diagnose IPF without a lung biopsy.
claims.locator: Raghu G, Remy-Jardin M, Richeldi L, et al., American Thoracic Society, European Respiratory Society, Japanese Respiratory Society and Asociación Latinoamericana de Tórax, American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine 205(9):e18-e47 (doi 10.1164/rccm.202202-0399ST), 'Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (an Update) and Progressive Pulmonary Fibrosis in Adults: An Official ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT Clinical Practice Guideline', published 1 May 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9851481/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **When tissue is needed, transbronchial lung cryobiopsy is an acceptable alternative to surgical lung biopsy in centres experienced with it** (conditional recommendation, very low-quality evidence). The panel could not agree for or against genomic classifier testing.
claims.locator: Raghu G, Remy-Jardin M, Richeldi L, et al., American Thoracic Society, European Respiratory Society, Japanese Respiratory Society and Asociación Latinoamericana de Tórax, American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine 205(9):e18-e47 (doi 10.1164/rccm.202202-0399ST), 'Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (an Update) and Progressive Pulmonary Fibrosis in Adults: An Official ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT Clinical Practice Guideline', published 1 May 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9851481/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Nintedanib and pirfenidone both slow lung-function decline in IPF**, roughly halving the rate of FVC decline, and are licensed in Australia for mild to moderate disease. Efficacy looks similar for the two.
claims.source_text: Two medications, nintedanib and pirfenidone, are effective in slowing the decline in lung function in IPF and are recommended for IPF in multinational clinical practice guidelines. These medications are licensed for the treatment of mild to moderate IPF (according to lung function criteria) in both Australia and New Zealand (Table 1). Both medications have been shown in randomized, double blind placebo controlled studies to slow the rate of decline in forced vital capacity (FVC) by approximately 50%., Pooled trial data and post hoc analyses suggest both drugs reduce the incidence of acute exacerbation. Efficacy appears to be similar for both medications.
claims.locator: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand (TSANZ), Respirology 2024, 'Treatment of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and progressive pulmonary fibrosis: A position statement from the Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand 2023 revision', published online 11 January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10952210/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Consider an anti-fibrotic for every patient at IPF diagnosis.** The decision to start or stop is individual: disease stage, preferences, comorbidities, toxicity risk and funding rules. Australia has no upper FVC limit for mild disease (New Zealand does, at FVC above 90%).
claims.source_text: Anti‐fibrotic therapy to slow IPF disease progression should be considered at IPF diagnosis in all patients. … The decision to start, and to stop, treatment with an anti‐fibrotic should be individualized, and is influenced by disease stage, patient preferences, consideration of comorbidities and risk of toxicity, plus local funding restrictions. … Funding is not currently available in New Zealand for mild disease with FVC greater than 90%, whereas no such limit applies in Australia.
claims.locator: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand (TSANZ), Respirology 2024, 'Treatment of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and progressive pulmonary fibrosis: A position statement from the Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand 2023 revision', published online 11 January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10952210/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Survival:** pooled trials showed pirfenidone cut all-cause death at 1 year by 48% (HR 0.52); for nintedanib the combined 12-month mortality HR was 0.69 (95%CI 0.44–1.07). Robust trial proof of long-term survival benefit is still lacking.
claims.source_text: pirfenidone reduced the risk of death from any cause at 1 year by 48% (hazard ratio [HR] 0.52; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.31-0.87; p = 0.01) … Combined data for the impact of nintedanib on 12 month all‐cause mortality demonstrated a HR 0.69 (95%CI 0.44-1.07). … Unfortunately, robust clinical trial data to confirm a long‐term survival benefit of anti‐fibrotic therapy are lacking.
claims.locator: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand (TSANZ), Respirology 2024, 'Treatment of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and progressive pulmonary fibrosis: A position statement from the Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand 2023 revision', published online 11 January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10952210/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Do not withhold treatment on age alone.** Nintedanib slowed FVC decline similarly in patients over 75 years and with multiple comorbidities; discontinuation was more common, but most tolerated it.
claims.source_text: A pooled analysis of five nintedanib clinical trials demonstrated similar slowing of FVC decline in IPF patients older than 75 years and in those with multiple co‐morbidities. Rates of AEs leading to treatment discontinuation were higher in those over 75 years and in those with multiple co‐morbidities, however, the majority of patients in these categories were able to tolerate nintedanib.
claims.locator: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand (TSANZ), Respirology 2024, 'Treatment of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and progressive pulmonary fibrosis: A position statement from the Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand 2023 revision', published online 11 January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10952210/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Severe disease:** post hoc data show benefit irrespective of baseline severity (including FVC <50% and/or DLCO <35%). Subsidised access may not cover severe impairment at baseline; whether to continue should weigh expected benefit against side effects and quality of life.
claims.source_text: post hoc analyses of ASCEND and RECAP trial data indicate benefit with pirfenidone across multiple domains in patients with FVC <50% and/or DLCO <35% … while access to anti‐fibrotic therapy may not be subsidized for patients with severe lung function impairment at baseline, the decision to continue anti‐fibrotic therapy should balance any anticipated benefit against potential negative impacts of anti‐fibrotic therapy (e.g., side effects) on quality of life.
claims.locator: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand (TSANZ), Respirology 2024, 'Treatment of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and progressive pulmonary fibrosis: A position statement from the Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand 2023 revision', published online 11 January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10952210/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Switch for toxicity, not for progression.** Funding permits switching between agents for intolerance, and many tolerate the alternative; there is no evidence switching helps disease progression, and it costs time off therapy.
claims.source_text: Many patients tolerate the alternative drug in the event of initial treatment toxicity. In New Zealand and Australia, funding authorities permit treatment switch between anti‐fibrotic agents for toxicity. There is no evidence that switching to an alternative anti‐fibrotic favourably impacts disease progression. Significant disease progression in an individual otherwise tolerating their current anti‐fibrotic agent should not necessarily prompt conversion to the other agent. The current anti‐fibrotic agents slow but do not stop disease progression. Switching treatments often leads to time off therapy, and potentially exposes patients to new intolerances.
claims.locator: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand (TSANZ), Respirology 2024, 'Treatment of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and progressive pulmonary fibrosis: A position statement from the Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand 2023 revision', published online 11 January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10952210/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Combination nintedanib plus pirfenidone is not recommended** outside clinical trials and is not subsidised in Australia or New Zealand.
claims.source_text: Combination anti‐fibrotic therapy is not currently recommended outside of clinical trials, nor is it subsidized in Australia or New Zealand.
claims.locator: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand (TSANZ), Respirology 2024, 'Treatment of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and progressive pulmonary fibrosis: A position statement from the Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand 2023 revision', published online 11 January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10952210/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Management pathway (S2):** consider antifibrotics (nintedanib, pirfenidone) together with oxygen and pulmonary rehabilitation; look for and treat pulmonary hypertension, reflux, obstructive sleep apnoea and lung cancer; involve palliative care for cough, breathlessness or anxiety; refer those at higher risk of death for transplant at diagnosis; and review for progression every 3–6 months or sooner.
claims.locator: Raghu G, Remy-Jardin M, Richeldi L, et al., American Thoracic Society, European Respiratory Society, Japanese Respiratory Society and Asociación Latinoamericana de Tórax, American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine 205(9):e18-e47 (doi 10.1164/rccm.202202-0399ST), 'Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (an Update) and Progressive Pulmonary Fibrosis in Adults: An Official ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT Clinical Practice Guideline', published 1 May 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9851481/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Acute exacerbation and respiratory failure (S2):** exacerbations may be treated with corticosteroids, and mechanical ventilation is not recommended for most patients with respiratory failure from IPF.
claims.locator: Raghu G, Remy-Jardin M, Richeldi L, et al., American Thoracic Society, European Respiratory Society, Japanese Respiratory Society and Asociación Latinoamericana de Tórax, American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine 205(9):e18-e47 (doi 10.1164/rccm.202202-0399ST), 'Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (an Update) and Progressive Pulmonary Fibrosis in Adults: An Official ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT Clinical Practice Guideline', published 1 May 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9851481/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Pirfenidone:** nausea (37.6%), diarrhoea (28.1%), dyspepsia, vomiting and photosensitive rash (25%) are the common effects. Counsel every patient on avoiding direct sun: broad-brimmed hat, long sleeves and 50+ sunscreen.
claims.source_text: Combined data from the pirfenidone studies report the most common AEs to be nausea (in 37.6% of patients), diarrhoea (28.1%), dyspepsia (18.4%), vomiting (15.9%) and photosensitive rash (25%) … All patients should be counselled regarding the avoidance of direct sunlight exposure and sun protection measures. … The risk of pirfenidone associated photosensitivity can be minimized by avoiding exposure to direct sunlight (including a broad brimmed hat and long‐sleeve shirts) and use of highly protective (50+) sunscreen.
claims.locator: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand (TSANZ), Respirology 2024, 'Treatment of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and progressive pulmonary fibrosis: A position statement from the Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand 2023 revision', published online 11 January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10952210/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Nintedanib:** diarrhoea is the main effect (about 60% vs 18% on placebo) but led to stopping in <5%. Manage with a low-fibre diet, avoiding spicy food, and loperamide. Take both drugs with meals.
claims.source_text: In the nintedanib studies, the most frequent AE was diarrhoea (with rates of approximately 60% compared to approximately 18% with placebo), which resulted in cessation of the drug in <5% of patients. … It is recommended that both pirfenidone and nintedanib are taken with meals to reduce the risk of gastrointestinal adverse effects. For nintedanib‐associated diarrhoea, dietary modification (including a low fibre diet and avoidance of spicy foods) coupled with the use of anti‐diarrhoeal medication (e.g., loperamide) can be helpful.
claims.locator: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand (TSANZ), Respirology 2024, 'Treatment of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and progressive pulmonary fibrosis: A position statement from the Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand 2023 revision', published online 11 January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10952210/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Monitor liver function after starting.** Serious ALT/AST rises occurred in 3.7% on pirfenidone (usually within 6 months) and 5% on nintedanib (mostly within 3 months), and reversed with dose reduction or interruption. Both are contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment; intolerance of one does not predict intolerance of the other.
claims.source_text: were observed in 3.7% of those taking pirfenidone in a pooled analysis of all trials. These abnormalities were typically observed within the first 6 months of treatment. Serious ALT/AST elevations occurred in 5% of nintedanib treated patients in the INPULSIS trials, with bilirubin elevations greater than two times the upper limit of normal in 0.5%, the majority of events occurring within the first 3 months of treatment. Reversal of the liver function derangement occurred with dose reduction/interruption of the anti‐fibrotic. Both anti‐fibrotics are contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment. Cautious monitoring of liver function is required after commencement of treatment as specified in the product information. If liver function derangement precludes continued use of one anti‐fibrotic, the other agent should be considered as intolerance of one does not predict intolerance to the other.
claims.locator: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand (TSANZ), Respirology 2024, 'Treatment of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and progressive pulmonary fibrosis: A position statement from the Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand 2023 revision', published online 11 January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10952210/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Check interactions:** pirfenidone is metabolised by CYP1A2, so avoid inhibitors such as ciprofloxacin and fluvoxamine (or reduce the dose substantially and monitor). Nintedanib levels can be affected by strong P-glycoprotein inducers or inhibitors.
claims.source_text: Pirfenidone is metabolized by CYP1A2, with inhibitors of this enzyme such as ciprofloxacin and fluvoxamine best avoided or otherwise associated with a substantial dose reduction and careful monitoring. Nintedanib is less prone to drug interactions, however, concentrations may be impacted by strong p‐glycoprotein inducers or inhibitors.
claims.locator: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand (TSANZ), Respirology 2024, 'Treatment of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and progressive pulmonary fibrosis: A position statement from the Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand 2023 revision', published online 11 January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10952210/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Dose reductions or interruptions help manage side effects,** and lower doses still appear to slow FVC decline, though the minimal effective dose is unknown.
claims.source_text: Temporary dose modifications, including dose reductions or interruptions, may also help in the management of AEs. In a pooled analysis from pirfenidone studies, a similar effect on FVC preservation was noted in patients who received either >90% or <90% of the expected pirfenidone treatment dose. Similar data have been reported for nintedanib. While these results suggest that a lower dose of pirfenidone or nintedanib remain effective in slowing FVC decline in IPF, the minimal effective dose is not clear.
claims.locator: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand (TSANZ), Respirology 2024, 'Treatment of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and progressive pulmonary fibrosis: A position statement from the Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand 2023 revision', published online 11 January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10952210/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **PPF is non-IPF ILD that progresses despite optimal treatment:** radiological fibrosis plus at least two of three over 12 months: worse symptoms, FVC decline ≥5% or DLCO ≥10%, or radiological progression. ⚠️ Australian PBS access to nintedanib also allows progression over 24 months (INBUILD criteria).
claims.source_text: PPF refers to non‐IPF ILD which is progressive despite treatment with optimal therapy. … It is defined as a patient with ILD of known or unknown aetiology other than IPF with radiological evidence of pulmonary fibrosis and clinical evidence of progression over the preceding 12 months. At least two of three criteria are required: 1. Worsening respiratory symptoms not otherwise explained; 2. Physiological evidence of disease progression, (absolute decline in FVC ≥5% or DLCO ≥10% over 12 months); and 3. Radiological evidence of disease progression, (such as increased traction bronchiectasis, bronchiolectasis, ground glass change with traction bronchiectasis, fine reticulation, reticular abnormality, honeycombing and volume loss). Notably, these criteria differ to the requirements for subsidized access to nintedanib in Australia for PPF, which also allow for progression to have been observed over 24 months, having been adopted from the INBUILD trial eligibility criteria for progressive fibrosing ILD (PF‐ILD) (Table 2).
claims.locator: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand (TSANZ), Respirology 2024, 'Treatment of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and progressive pulmonary fibrosis: A position statement from the Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand 2023 revision', published online 11 January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10952210/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Fibrotic ILDs that can behave as PPF (S2 Table 5):** idiopathic fibrotic NSIP, pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis, fibrosing organising pneumonia, desquamative interstitial pneumonia, fibrotic CTD-related ILD, fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis, fibrotic occupational lung disease (such as asbestosis or silicosis), fibrotic Langerhans cell histiocytosis, fibrotic sarcoidosis, unclassifiable fibrotic ILD (a label to use only after multidisciplinary discussion) and others, such as inborn errors of metabolism or surfactant protein disorders.
claims.locator: Raghu G, Remy-Jardin M, Richeldi L, et al., American Thoracic Society, European Respiratory Society, Japanese Respiratory Society and Asociación Latinoamericana de Tórax, American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine 205(9):e18-e47 (doi 10.1164/rccm.202202-0399ST), 'Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (an Update) and Progressive Pulmonary Fibrosis in Adults: An Official ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT Clinical Practice Guideline', published 1 May 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9851481/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Progression should prompt diagnostic reassessment.** Some progressive ILDs are still best treated with immunosuppression (e.g. CTD-ILD) or antigen avoidance (fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis), possibly with nintedanib added.
claims.source_text: Disease progression in non‐IPF ILDs should prompt reassessment of diagnostic classification and consideration of the role of other disease modifying therapies. … Despite demonstrating progressive disease behaviour, certain ILDs may still be best treated with immunosuppression such as CTD‐ILD, or antigen avoidance in fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis, potentially alongside the addition of nintedanib
claims.locator: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand (TSANZ), Respirology 2024, 'Treatment of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and progressive pulmonary fibrosis: A position statement from the Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand 2023 revision', published online 11 January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10952210/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Nintedanib should be considered in PPF.** In INBUILD (non-IPF fibrosis >10% of lung on CT, progressing within 24 months) FVC fell 80.8 mL/year on nintedanib vs 187.8 mL/year on placebo, consistently across subgroups; it is approved in Australia for PPF.
claims.source_text: Nintedanib should be considered in patients with PPF, with evidence for treatment benefit across a range of ILD subgroups. … Patients were required to have non‐IPF fibrosing lung disease affecting greater than 10% of lung volume on CT and evidence of progression despite management within the preceding 24 months. This study showed that nintedanib was beneficial, with patients on treatment declining in FVC by 80.8 mL/year compared with 187.8 mL/year in the placebo group … is now approved in Australia for use in patients with PPF
claims.locator: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand (TSANZ), Respirology 2024, 'Treatment of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and progressive pulmonary fibrosis: A position statement from the Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand 2023 revision', published online 11 January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10952210/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Pirfenidone has no local approval or guideline recommendation for PPF;** only low-quality evidence suggests benefit.
claims.source_text: Pirfenidone, on the other hand, has not received local approval or guideline recommendations for use in PPF, based on the current evidence. … Low quality evidence suggests a treatment benefit for pirfenidone in PPF.
claims.locator: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand (TSANZ), Respirology 2024, 'Treatment of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and progressive pulmonary fibrosis: A position statement from the Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand 2023 revision', published online 11 January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10952210/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Measure decline as absolute, not relative, change** (S2): from an FVC of 60% predicted, progression is reached at 55%, not 57%; DLCO needs an absolute fall of 10% or more. Exclude other explanations first, particularly for worsening symptoms or DLCO. PPF is a disease behaviour, not a diagnosis.
claims.locator: Raghu G, Remy-Jardin M, Richeldi L, et al., American Thoracic Society, European Respiratory Society, Japanese Respiratory Society and Asociación Latinoamericana de Tórax, American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine 205(9):e18-e47 (doi 10.1164/rccm.202202-0399ST), 'Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (an Update) and Progressive Pulmonary Fibrosis in Adults: An Official ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT Clinical Practice Guideline', published 1 May 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9851481/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **S2's treatment recommendations for PPF:** nintedanib is suggested once standard management of the underlying fibrotic ILD has failed (conditional, low-quality evidence); for pirfenidone it made only a research recommendation, because about a third of the panel abstained.
claims.locator: Raghu G, Remy-Jardin M, Richeldi L, et al., American Thoracic Society, European Respiratory Society, Japanese Respiratory Society and Asociación Latinoamericana de Tórax, American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine 205(9):e18-e47 (doi 10.1164/rccm.202202-0399ST), 'Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (an Update) and Progressive Pulmonary Fibrosis in Adults: An Official ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT Clinical Practice Guideline', published 1 May 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9851481/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Repeat HRCT when fibrosis seems to be worsening;** the best interval is unknown. A yearly HRCT can be considered to screen for complications, especially lung cancer.
claims.locator: Raghu G, Remy-Jardin M, Richeldi L, et al., American Thoracic Society, European Respiratory Society, Japanese Respiratory Society and Asociación Latinoamericana de Tórax, American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine 205(9):e18-e47 (doi 10.1164/rccm.202202-0399ST), 'Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (an Update) and Progressive Pulmonary Fibrosis in Adults: An Official ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT Clinical Practice Guideline', published 1 May 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9851481/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Acute exacerbation of IPF has no proven therapy** and a poor prognosis: supportive care, oxygen, and cover for possible infection. High-dose corticosteroids are common but unproven, and anti-fibrotics have no proven role for starting in the acute setting.
claims.source_text: There remain no proven therapies for AE‐IPF. Management consists of supportive care with a focus on palliation of symptoms, supplemental oxygen to correct hypoxaemia and consideration of broad spectrum antibiotics and/or antiviral agents to cover possible infection. … The prognosis of AE‐IPF is poor. … Corticosteroids, typically in high doses, are frequently utilized in the management of AE‐IPF, but data on efficacy are lacking. … have no proven role for initiation in the acute setting.
claims.locator: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand (TSANZ), Respirology 2024, 'Treatment of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and progressive pulmonary fibrosis: A position statement from the Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand 2023 revision', published online 11 January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10952210/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Criteria for acute exacerbation of IPF (S1 Table 4):** acute respiratory deterioration, typically lasting under 1 month, in someone with IPF, with new bilateral ground-glass opacity and/or consolidation on CT, not explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload, once extra-parenchymal causes (such as pneumothorax, pleural effusion or pulmonary embolism) are excluded.
claims.source_text: [TABLE 4] Criteria for acute exacerbation of IPF. [TABLE 4 row 1] Acute respiratory deterioration of typically <1 month duration in someone with IPF: Extra‐parenchymal cause excluded (e.g., pneumothorax, pleural effusion, pulmonary embolism) [TABLE 4 row 2] Acute respiratory deterioration of typically <1 month duration in someone with IPF: New, bilateral ground glass opacity and/or consolidation on CT [TABLE 4 row 3] Acute respiratory deterioration of typically <1 month duration in someone with IPF: Not explained by congestive cardiac failure of fluid overload
claims.locator: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand (TSANZ), Respirology 2024, 'Treatment of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and progressive pulmonary fibrosis: A position statement from the Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand 2023 revision', published online 11 January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10952210/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Reflux treatment does not improve IPF respiratory outcomes;** treat symptomatic reflux as for the general population.
claims.source_text: There is insufficient evidence to support a beneficial role of anti‐acid pharmacotherapy or surgery for respiratory outcomes in patients with IPF. … Symptomatic gastro‐oesophageal reflux should be approached per clinical guidelines for the general population.
claims.locator: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand (TSANZ), Respirology 2024, 'Treatment of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and progressive pulmonary fibrosis: A position statement from the Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand 2023 revision', published online 11 January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10952210/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **S2 agrees and goes further:** it suggests against antacid medicines and against antireflux surgery (complications in up to 15%) when the only aim is better respiratory outcomes (both conditional, very low-quality evidence); surgery may still suit reflux-related problems.
claims.locator: Raghu G, Remy-Jardin M, Richeldi L, et al., American Thoracic Society, European Respiratory Society, Japanese Respiratory Society and Asociación Latinoamericana de Tórax, American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine 205(9):e18-e47 (doi 10.1164/rccm.202202-0399ST), 'Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (an Update) and Progressive Pulmonary Fibrosis in Adults: An Official ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT Clinical Practice Guideline', published 1 May 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9851481/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Ambrisentan, bosentan and riociguat are contraindicated in pulmonary hypertension with IPF.**
claims.source_text: Ambrisentan, bosentan and riociguat are contraindicated in PH associated with IPF.

claims.claim: **Vasodilator trials in IPF and ILD (S1 Table 5):** only inhaled treprostinil helped, in ILD with catheter-proven pulmonary hypertension (INCREASE, 326 patients: 6MWD up 31.12 m at 16 weeks, with better NT-proBNP and less clinical worsening). Sildenafil (STEP-IPF; INSTAGE with nintedanib; with pirfenidone) and bosentan (BPHIT) showed no benefit; riociguat (RISE-IIP) was stopped early for more serious adverse events, including deaths; ambrisentan (ARTEMIS-IPF) increased disease progression (27.4% v 17.2%; hazard ratio 1.74).
claims.source_text: [TABLE 5] Recent seminal studies with vasodilator therapies in IPF and other ILD cohorts. [TABLE 5 row 1] Study: INCREASE Treprostinil Versus placebo Phase 2/3 · Year: 2021 · Population: ILD with PH confirmed by right heart catheter · Number patients: 326 · Primary endpoint: Change in 6MWD at 16‐weeks · Outcome: Improved 6MWD in treatment arm of 31.12 m (95% CI, 16.85-45.39; p < 0.001); improved NT‐proBNP, reduced clinical worsening, compared with control arm. [TABLE 5 row 2] Study: Sildenafil plus pirfenidone versus placebo plus pirfenidone Phase 2b · Year: 2021 · Population: IPF with DLCO ≤40% predicted and mPAP ≥20 mm Hg · Number patients: 177 · Primary endpoint: Proportion with disease progression (change in 6MWD, respiratory hospitalization, death) at 52‐weeks · Outcome: No difference in the primary endpoint, between‐group difference 3.06% (95% CI -11.30 to 17.97; p = 0.65). [TABLE 5 row 3] Study: RISE‐IIP Riociguat versus placebo Phase 2b · Year: 2019 · Population: IIP with PH confirmed by right heart catheter · Number patients: 147 · Primary endpoint: Change in 6MWD at 26‐weeks · Outcome: No difference in the primary endpoint or time to clinical worsening; trial terminated early due to increased SAEs including death in treatment arm. [TABLE 5 row 4] Study: INSTAGE Sildenafil plus nintedanib versus placebo plus nintedanib Phase 3 · Year: 2018 · Population: IPF patients with DLCO ≤35% predicted · Number patients: 274 · Primary endpoint: Change in baseline total SGRQ score at 12‐weeks · Outcome: No difference in mean change in SGRQ score (treatment arm -1.28 points, control arm -0.77 points; p = 0.72). No difference in dyspnoea scores or safety. [TABLE 5 row 5] Study: BPHIT Bosentan versus placebo Phase 2 · Year: 2014 · Population: Fibrotic IIP with right heart catheter confirmed PH · Number patients: 60 · Primary endpoint: Fall from baseline pulmonary vascular resistance index of 20% or more at 16 weeks · Outcome: No difference in invasive pulmonary haemodynamics, functional capacity or symptoms. [TABLE 5 row 6] Study: ARTEMIS‐IPF Ambrisentan versus placebo Phase 3 · Year: 2013 · Population: IPF patients with ≤5% honeycombing on HRCT scan · Number patients: 492 · Primary endpoint: Time to disease progression (death, respiratory hospitalization, decrease in FVC and DLCO); 48‐week assessment · Outcome: Increased disease progression in treatment arm (90 [27.4%] vs. 28 [17.2%] patients; p < 0.010; hazard ratio, 1.74 [95% CI, 1.14-2.66]) [TABLE 5 row 7] Study: STEP‐IPF Sildenafil versus placebo Phase 3 · Year: 2010 · Population: IPF patients with DLCO ≤35% predicted · Number patients: 180 · Primary endpoint: Proportion of patients with an increase in 6MWD ≥20% · Outcome: No difference in proportion meeting primary endpoint (treatment arm 10%, control arm 7%; p = 0.39); some secondary endpoints improved with treatment

claims.claim: **Features suggesting short telomeres in pulmonary fibrosis (S1 Table 6):** a family history of ILD, diagnosis before age 50, nail dystrophy, premature greying (before 25), a personal or family history of blood-count abnormalities (macrocytosis, thrombocytopenia), and a personal or family history of unexplained liver disease.
claims.source_text: [TABLE 6] Features suggestive of shortened telomeres in a patient with pulmonary fibrosis. [TABLE 6 row 1] Positive family history of ILD: Age of diagnosis under 50 years [TABLE 6 row 2] Positive family history of ILD: Nail dystrophy [TABLE 6 row 3] Positive family history of ILD: Premature hair greying (before 25 years) [TABLE 6 row 4] Positive family history of ILD: Personal or family history of full blood count abnormalities (macrocytosis, thrombocytopenia) [TABLE 6 row 5] Positive family history of ILD: Personal or family history of unexplained liver disease

claims.claim: **Shortened telomeres raise the risk of harm from immunosuppression;** use it cautiously in these patients.
claims.source_text: IPF patients with shortened telomeres are at heightened risk of harm from immunosuppression. Caution should be exercised when considering immunosuppression in this patient group.

claims.claim: **Refer every ILD patient early for pulmonary rehabilitation,** and consider repeating it if symptoms progress.
claims.source_text: Early referral for pulmonary rehabilitation is strongly encouraged for all patients with ILD, and consideration should be given to repeating pulmonary rehabilitation if symptoms progress.

claims.claim: **Refer early for transplant assessment**, since the disease course is hard to predict. Continue the anti-fibrotic while waiting, if the transplant centre agrees.
claims.source_text: Early referral for pre‐transplant assessment is essential, as it is difficult to accurately predict disease trajectory. … should be continued in most patients awaiting transplantation, so long as this is supported by the transplant centre.

claims.claim: **Offer every patient with IPF or PPF the option of a clinical trial.**
claims.source_text: All patients with IPF and PPF should be presented with the option to participate in clinical trials.
